1037.title: the mudras
1037.hook: a raised open palm on a temple image, and a lowered one beneath it: two hands that speak first
1037.carry: the raised palm that says do not fear
1037.howItsDone: Devotees meet abhaya and varada mudras on the images of deities in temples and home shrines; the raised open palm is read as "do not fear" and the lowered open palm as the giving of blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday the mudras gave the hand a job: steering the breath, one nostril, then the other. Did your hand find its place at the nose? Now the hands turn around and face you. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

A crossing guard steps into the road and lifts one hand, palm out, fingers up. The cars stop. Nobody says anything. The hand says it all. Now stand in front of an image of Shiva as the dancer, ringed in flame. Among his hands, one is raised, open, palm toward you, fingers up. Almost the crossing guard's hand. But it isn't saying stop. It's saying something gentler. So far the mudras have been things a practitioner does. Today, two mudras you don't make. You receive them.
screen: `ONE RAISED PALM STOPS THE TRAFFIC.` → `THE SAME PALM ON SHIVA.` → `A MUDRA YOU RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: That raised, open palm is called abhaya mudra. Abhaya means fearlessness, the absence of fear. The gesture says: do not be afraid. On some images there's a second hand to look for, lowered, palm open toward you, fingers pointing down, as if letting something fall into your hands. That one is varada mudra, the gesture of giving, of granting what is asked. In some paintings of Lakshmi, coins pour from that lowered palm. One hand lifts the fear. The other hand gives. Now open the Bhagavad Gita to its sixteenth chapter. Krishna lists the qualities of a person whose nature leans toward the divine, and the list begins with one word: abhayam, fearlessness. Then purity of heart, steadiness in knowledge, giving, self-control. Fearlessness opens the list. So when a devotee stands before an image with that hand raised, the very quality the Gita names at the head of its list is being held out to them. People read the gesture in more than one way. Some hear a promise: the god protects, there is nothing to fear here. Some hear an invitation: this is a quality meant to grow in the one who looks. The palm holds both readings at once. One more detail: the same raised palm and the same lowered, giving hand also appear on Buddhist and Jain images, each tradition reading them in its own way. A shared language of hands. Which turns the mudras around. They aren't only something you form in a quiet room. They are also something offered to you. You stand in front of a hand, and it speaks first.
screen: `ABHAYA: THE PALM THAT SAYS DO NOT FEAR.` · `VARADA: THE LOWERED PALM THAT GIVES.` · `GITA 16: THE LIST OPENS WITH FEARLESSNESS.` · `A PROMISE, OR AN INVITATION.` · then, large: `THE HAND SPEAKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let the left hand hang loosely beside the left knee, palm open and turned forward, fingers pointing down toward the floor. That's the giving hand. Raise the right hand to about shoulder height, palm facing forward, fingers up, relaxed rather than stiff. That's the hand that says do not fear. Hold both, and breathe slowly. If a worry comes to mind, let it sit in front of the raised palm. Don't argue with it. Just let it meet the hand. If you pray, you can hold the gesture facing a home shrine. If you don't, simply let the two hands rest in their shapes and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Today, two you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the lowered palm that gives.

Your line: the raised palm that says do not fear. Today, when someone near you is anxious, notice your own hands before you speak. Let them be open and unhurried, and see what they say before your words do. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

1038.title: the mudras
1038.hook: a dancer tells a whole story with her hands, and an old dance manual says where the hand goes, the eyes follow
1038.carry: where the hand goes, the eyes follow
1038.howItsDone: In classical Indian dance forms such as Bharatanatyam, dancers learn named hand gestures (hastas) and use them with facial expression to tell stories, often of the gods, before an audience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the lowered palm that gives. When someone was anxious near you, what did your hands do? Today the hands start to move. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

How do you say lotus without a word? A dancer on a temple stage cups her hand, fingers curved and spread, and there it is, a flower opening. A turn of the wrist, and two fingers become a deer's ears. The hand flattens, fingers together, thumb tucked, and now it's a flag, or a cloud, or a forest, depending on the story she's telling. The drum keeps time. Her face follows her hands. Anyone who knows the language of the hands can follow without a program. Today the mudras leave the meditation cushion and walk onto a stage.
screen: `A LOTUS, WITHOUT A WORD.` → `A FLAG, A CLOUD, A FOREST.` → `THE FACE FOLLOWS THE HANDS.`

segments.voice: In classical Indian dance, the hand gestures have their own name: hastas, hands. Dancers call them mudras too. One old manual for dancers is the Abhinaya Darpana, the mirror of gesture, attributed to a teacher named Nandikeshvara. It lists hand shapes one by one, each with a name and a list of meanings. Pataka, the flag: the flat hand, fingers together, thumb bent in. Mukula, the bud. Bhramara, the bee. Hamsasya, the swan's beak. One shape can stand for many things, and the story around it tells you which. Then comes a verse that dancers quote, here in paraphrase. Where the hand goes, the eyes follow. Where the eyes go, the mind follows. Where the mind goes, the feeling follows. And where the feeling goes, rasa arises. Rasa means juice, flavor, taste. In the old theory of drama, it's the feeling the audience tastes when a performance works. So the chain runs from a hand, to the eyes, to the mind, to a feeling, to something the whole room shares. Notice the direction. On a meditation cushion, you might think the mind leads and the hand obeys. The dancer's verse runs it the other way: start with the hand, and the rest of you comes along. And the same manual opens by bowing to Shiva, in paraphrase: whose body is the whole world, whose speech is all language, whose ornaments are the moon and stars. For the dancer, the stage is a small copy of that. A hand moving in the light becomes a way of speaking about the world, and to the one who dances it.
screen: `HASTAS: THE DANCER'S HANDS.` · `A FLAG, A BUD, A BEE, A SWAN'S BEAK.` · `HAND, EYES, MIND, FEELING, RASA.` · `THE HAND LEADS, THE REST FOLLOWS.` · then, large: `WHERE THE HAND GOES, THE EYES FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Sit up, with room in front of you. Make pataka, the flag: right hand flat, fingers together, thumb bent in. Hold it in front of your chest. Now move it, very slowly, out to the right, and let your eyes follow the hand. Only the hand and the eyes. Bring it slowly back to center, eyes still with it. Then out to the left, and back. Go slower than feels natural. Notice whether the mind follows the eyes, the way the verse says, or wanders off somewhere else. When it wanders, return to the hand. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. In dance, hastas: hand shapes that tell a story, and a verse that says where the hand goes, the eyes, the mind and the feeling follow.

Your line: where the hand goes, the eyes follow. Today, once, when your attention scatters, give it a hand to follow: trace one slow line in the air, eyes on your fingertips, and see where the mind goes. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

1039.title: the mudras
1039.hook: a potter's hands, a cook's, a shopkeeper's: no sacred shape among them, and the Gita puts hands everywhere
1039.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1039.howItsDone: Hindus hold shaped hands in worship, practice and dance; some also reflect on Bhagavad Gita 13 and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, which describe the one reality as having hands and feet everywhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday the mudras went on stage: a dancer's hand, and the verse that says where the hand goes, the eyes follow. When your attention scattered, did a slow hand bring it back? Today, the last day of the mudras, and the widest view of the hand. Day one thousand thirty-nine.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `WHERE THE HAND GOES, THE EYES FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: A potter's wheel turns in a narrow lane. Two wet hands close around a lump of clay, and it rises between them into a wall, then a lip, then a bowl. Next door, a woman's hands press dough flat and slap it onto a hot pan. Across the lane, a shopkeeper's hands count out change. Nobody here is holding a sacred shape. Nobody is on a stage. All week the mudras have been hands that mean something on purpose. Today the Gita takes the hand as wide as it can go, and puts hands everywhere.
screen: `A POTTER'S HANDS. A COOK'S. A SHOPKEEPER'S.` → `NO SACRED SHAPE.` → `HANDS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: In the thirteenth chapter of the Gita, Krishna describes what is to be known, the one reality behind everything. And the description begins with hands. In paraphrase: its hands and feet are everywhere; its eyes, heads and faces are everywhere; its ears are everywhere; it stands in the world, enfolding all. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad carries the same line, almost word for word. Then the next verse turns it around, in paraphrase: it shines through the workings of all the senses, and yet it is without senses; unattached, and yet it holds everything up. Both halves matter. Hands everywhere. And no hands at all. Readers hold the two together in different ways. Some commentators say it is spoken of as having hands because of the hands of all beings, through which it works, while it is never bound to any one of them. Some devotees hear something closer to home: the divine at work in every pair of hands. The verse leaves room for both. Now look back at the week of hands. A seal, pressed in so it holds. Anjali, the joined palms, a bow to you. Chin mudra, the small self bending to touch the great, under a banyan tree. The breathing hand at the nose. Abhaya and varada, the palms on an image that say do not fear, and give. The dancer's hand, with the eyes and the mind following. Each was a hand shaped to carry a meaning. The Gita's line doesn't cancel any of that. It widens it. The shaped hand before a shrine, and the hand at the wheel or the stove or the counter, are named in one breath: hands everywhere. A mudra holds a meaning on purpose. Some readers take this verse to say that every hand at work is already held inside a larger one.
screen: `GITA 13: HANDS AND FEET EVERYWHERE.` · `THE NEXT VERSE: AND WITHOUT SENSES.` · `THE WEEK OF SHAPED HANDS.` · `THE SHRINE AND THE STOVE, IN ONE BREATH.` · then, large: `HANDS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest the hands on the thighs, palms up. Look at them for a breath or two: the lines, the knuckles, the places that do the work. Then close the eyes. Bring to mind other hands that were part of your day: hands that grew the food you ate, carried it, cooked it, built the chair beneath you. Let each pair come and go, without a story. Then let the attention settle back into your own open palms. If you pray, you can let the verse rest there: hands everywhere. If not, simply stay with the warmth of the palms and the breath. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Today, the widest one: the Gita's line that what is to be known has hands and feet everywhere, and the next verse, that it is without senses.

Your line: hands and feet everywhere. Today, notice one pair of hands at work that isn't yours, a cook's, a driver's, a cashier's, and watch them for a moment as if they were making a mudra. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1040.hook: in the Gita Krishna says that among letters he is the first one, a, the sound of an open mouth
1040.carry: listen for the a inside it
1040.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1040.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn the alphabet aloud, in its traditional order from vowels to consonants grouped by where the mouth makes them, often reciting it with a teacher before reading texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the mudras with the Gita's widest picture: hands and feet everywhere, and yet no senses at all. Did you watch someone's hands at work? Today the mouth takes over from the hands. Day one thousand forty.

Open a careful English edition of the Gita and the names start to grow small marks. A line over a letter. A dot underneath. An accent perched on an s. It is easy to skip the marks, say the word the way it looks in English, and keep going. But every one of those marks is a direction for the mouth. They're how a page of English letters carries a language that was built to be heard. This week, one alphabet, learned the way it was meant to be learned: by sound.
screen: `A LINE OVER, A DOT UNDER.` → `EVERY MARK IS A DIRECTION.` → `AN ALPHABET LEARNED BY SOUND.`

segments.voice: Start with a verse. In the tenth chapter of the Gita, Krishna names, kind by kind, where he can be found. Among rivers, the Ganga. Among trees, the sacred fig. And at verse thirty-three, in paraphrase: among letters, I am the letter a. Not a grand letter. The plainest one. The sound you make when you open your mouth and let the voice out without shaping it at all. A. That letter is where the Sanskrit alphabet begins, and the whole order is a journey from there. The vowels come first. Then the consonants, arranged not at random, but by where in the mouth they're made, moving forward from the throat toward the lips. Say the alphabet in order and the sound walks out of you. There's a second gift in that small letter. In Devanagari, the script Sanskrit is often written in today, a consonant on its own already carries a short a inside it. The letter for k is read ka. The letter for m is read ma. Unless a mark tells you otherwise, the a is there, quietly, in almost every letter on the page. So Krishna's line has a reader's meaning too: the plainest sound runs through all the others. At least one Upanishad treats pronunciation as something to be taught with care. The Taittiriya Upanishad opens a lesson by announcing it: now we will explain shiksha, the teaching of sound, and lists what that teaching covers: the letter, the pitch, the length, the effort, the evenness, the joining. That's this week. Not grammar. Not vocabulary. Just the sounds, so the names you already read can be said the way they were heard.
screen: `GITA 10.33: AMONG LETTERS, I AM A.` · `FROM THE THROAT TOWARD THE LIPS.` · `A HIDES INSIDE EVERY CONSONANT.` · `SHIKSHA: THE TEACHING OF SOUND.` · then, large: `THE PLAINEST SOUND RUNS THROUGH ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, and let the jaw soften. Breathe in through the nose. On the out-breath, open the mouth a little and let a quiet sound come out with no shaping at all: a. Like the beginning of the word about. Let it last as long as the breath does, soft, not loud. Then breathe in again. Notice where the sound seems to come from: the throat, the chest, somewhere behind the mouth. Keep going, one a on each out-breath, and between them, silence. If sound isn't possible where you are, say it inwardly. The bell holds the time.
A. The open mouth, the plainest sound, the letter Krishna names in the Gita, hidden inside almost every letter on the page.
Your line: listen for the a inside it. Today, catch one Sanskrit name you read or hear, Rama, Shiva, karma, and listen for the a inside it. Day one thousand forty.

1041.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1041.hook: a small line over one letter in Rāma tells the voice to stay longer there
1041.carry: let one long vowel be long
1041.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1041.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn short and long vowels as pairs, and reciters of verses keep the lengths carefully, since the rhythm of a verse depends on them.

segments.voice: Yesterday began Sanskrit sounds for readers with the plainest letter, a, the one Krishna names in the Gita, hidden in almost every consonant. Did you listen for the a inside it? Today, the same sound, held longer. Day one thousand forty-one.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `A: THE OPEN MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Write the name of the prince of Ayodhya in careful English letters and it looks like this: R, a with a small line over it, m, a. Rāma. The line sits on the first a only. The second a has nothing. It's a tiny mark, easy to treat as decoration, easy for the eye to slide right over. But it's an instruction about time. It tells the voice where to stay and where to move on. Today, the line over the letter.
screen: `RĀMA: A LINE OVER ONE A.` → `NOT DECORATION.` → `AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT TIME.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's Upanishad listed what the teaching of sound covers, and one item on that list was matra: length, the measure of a sound in time. Sanskrit vowels come in short and long pairs. Short a, long ā. Short i, long ī. Short u, long ū. In Devanagari the long vowel has its own letter or sign. In English transliteration, it gets a small line on top. So that line means: hold this one longer. The tradition of reciting measures this in units it calls matras: a short vowel takes one, a long vowel about two. Now listen to names you already know. Rāma: the first syllable long, the second short. Rah-muh. Sītā: both vowels long. See-tah. Gītā, as in the Bhagavad Gita: also both long, so the name ends on an open ah, not a clipped uh. And then words where nothing is long. Karma: both short. Kur-muh. Shiva: both short. Shi-vuh. Nothing is wrong with how English speakers say these names; anyone who hears them will know who you mean. But the length changes the music. Much Sanskrit verse is measured in light and heavy syllables, and vowel length helps decide which is which, so length is part of a line's rhythm, the way beats are part of a song. Stretch the wrong syllable and a chanted verse starts to limp. Get the lengths right and the line walks the way it was made to walk. That's why the little line matters to a reader. It isn't about sounding impressive. It's a way of hearing the text as its reciters heard it, one measured breath of sound after another.
screen: `MATRA: LENGTH, A SOUND'S MEASURE IN TIME.` · `SHORT A, LONG Ā. SHORT I, LONG Ī.` · `RĀMA, SĪTĀ, GĪTĀ. KARMA, SHIVA.` · `LENGTH IS PART OF THE RHYTHM.` · then, large: `THE LINE MEANS: STAY LONGER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe in. On the out-breath, say a short a, quick and soft, then a long ā, held about twice as long. Breathe in. Do it again. Feel the difference in the body: one is a step, the other is a stride. Then try a name you know. Rāma: long, then short. Sītā: long, then long. Say each slowly, letting the line over the letter decide how long you stay. If you pray, you can let a name you pray with carry this rhythm. If not, just listen to the measure. The bell holds the time.
Matra. The length of a sound in time: short and long vowels, and the small line over a letter that means stay longer.
Your line: let one long vowel be long. Today, when you see a line over a letter, slow down on it, and let one long vowel be long. Day one thousand forty-one.

1042.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1042.hook: ka, cha, ta, ta, pa: say the consonant rows in order and the sound walks from the throat to the lips
1042.carry: find where in the mouth it lives
1042.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1042.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit recite the consonants row by row, ka-kha-ga-gha-nga and onward, learning each row by where the mouth makes it, from the throat to the lips.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Sanskrit sounds for readers, the line over a letter: a long vowel, stay longer. Rāma, long then short. Did you let one long vowel be long? Today the consonants, and a map of the mouth. Day one thousand forty-two.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE LINE MEANS: STAY LONGER.`

segments.voice: A chakra, in a scholar's book, is spelled c, a, k, r, a. Cakra. A reader who has heard the word chakra all their life stops and frowns. Did someone drop a letter? No. In the careful system of spelling Sanskrit in English letters, c is always said ch, as in church. It looks like a typo until you know the map behind it. And the map behind it is worth having: the consonants laid out in rows, each row a place in your own mouth.
screen: `CAKRA, NOT A TYPO.` → `C IS ALWAYS CH.` → `A MAP OF THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the map. Say each sound slowly as it comes, and feel where it lands. The first row is made at the back, in the throat: ka, kha, ga, gha, and a nasal, nga. The second row moves forward to the palate, where the middle of the tongue rises: cha, chha, ja, jha, and nya. The third row is made with the tip of the tongue curled up to the roof of the mouth. We'll spend tomorrow on that one. The fourth row comes forward again, the tongue touching the teeth: ta, tha, da, dha, na. And the last row is made at the lips: pa, pha, ba, bha, ma. Throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips. Say the first sound of each row in order, ka, cha, ta, ta, pa, and the sound walks forward out of you, from the back of the mouth to the front. Every row ends the same way, with a sound that hums through the nose. And inside each row, plain sounds sit beside breathy ones, ka beside kha; that pattern gets its own day soon. The Upanishad's list for the teaching of sound starts with the letter, varna, and laid out this way the alphabet is more than a list to memorize. It's a description of the body speaking. For a reader, this map does real work. It explains why c is ch: it lives in the palate row. Cakra is chakra. Candra, the moon, is chandra. And it means that when you meet a strange spelling, you can ask one useful question: where in the mouth does this sound live? Find the place, and the sound usually follows.
screen: `THROAT: KA. PALATE: CHA.` · `ROOF, THEN TEETH: TA, TA.` · `LIPS: PA. EACH ROW ENDS IN A HUM.` · `C IS CH: CAKRA IS CHAKRA.` · then, large: `WHERE IN THE MOUTH DOES IT LIVE?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, mouth relaxed. On one out-breath, say slowly: ka. Feel it at the back of the throat. Next breath: cha. Feel the middle of the tongue rise. Next: ta, with the tongue curled back. Next: ta, at the teeth. Next: pa, at the lips. Then rest for a breath, and walk the sounds forward again: ka, cha, ta, ta, pa. Go slowly enough to feel each place. Then end with the hum that closes the last row, softly, ma, at the lips, and let it fade into the breath. The bell holds the time.
Ka. The first consonant, made in the throat, where the map of the mouth begins: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips, and c always said ch.
Your line: find where in the mouth it lives. Today, catch one word you say often and ask where in the mouth its first sound lives. Day one thousand forty-two.

1043.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1043.hook: Krishna in a scholar's book carries a dot under the r, the s and the n, and each dot curls the tongue
1043.carry: let your tongue curl back for it
1043.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1043.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit practice the retroflex row (ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa) by curling the tongue back to the roof of the mouth, and recite names like Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu with these sounds.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Sanskrit sounds for readers, ka, the first consonant, and ka, the first consonant, and ka, the first consonant, and the map of the mouth: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips, and c always said ch. We skipped the roof. Today we go there, and look back on the week. Day one thousand forty-three.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THROAT, PALATE, ROOF, TEETH, LIPS.`

segments.voice: Krishna, the way a scholar spells it, has dots hanging under its letters. K. R with a dot. S with a dot. N with a dot. A. Kṛṣṇa. It can look fussy, like footnotes that wandered into the middle of a word. But the dots point to the place we skipped yesterday, the roof of the mouth. They tell the tongue to do one thing: curl back. Today, the dot underneath.
screen: `KṚṢṆA: A DOT UNDER R, S AND N.` → `NOT FOOTNOTES.` → `THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.`

segments.voice: Put the tip of your tongue behind your top teeth and say ta. That's the teeth row. Now slide the tip back along the roof of your mouth, past the ridge, and curl it up a little. Say ta from there. The sound gets deeper, almost hollow. That's the roof row, and in transliteration its letters get a dot underneath: ṭa, ḍa, ṇa. Linguists call these sounds retroflex: made with the tongue bent back. The same curl gives a second kind of sh. Plain sh, written with an accent mark on the s, sits at the palate: Śiva. The s with a dot under it is sh said with the tongue curled back: Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa. And the r with a dot under it is something else again: a vowel. Sanskrit treats a lightly rolled r as a vowel sound in its own right, ṛ. How it's said depends on where you learned it. Some reciters say it close to ri, which is where the English spelling Krishna comes from. Others, in parts of the south and west, say it closer to ru. Both are living ways of saying the same letter. So now the name can be read in full: kṛ, with the r-vowel; ṣ, the curled sh; ṇa, the curled n. And look at the week behind us. The mudras ended with hands that were received, danced, and found everywhere. Then the sounds began: a, the plainest letter; the line that says stay longer; the map of the mouth; and today, the dot that curls the tongue. Hands, then mouth. Each one a way of letting the body carry meaning.
screen: `THE ROOF ROW: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.` · `Ś AT THE PALATE, Ṣ CURLED BACK.` · `Ṛ: THE R THAT IS A VOWEL.` · `THE WEEK: HANDS, THEN MOUTH.` · then, large: `THE DOT MEANS: CURL THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let the jaw hang soft. On an out-breath, say ta at the teeth. Next breath, curl the tongue back and say ṭa at the roof. Go back and forth slowly, a few times, feeling the tongue travel. Then the n: na at the teeth, ṇa at the roof. Then put it together and say the name slowly, piece by piece: kṛ, ṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa. However you've always said it is fine. This is just listening to what the dots ask for. If you pray, you can let the name be said with care. If not, simply notice the tongue at work. The bell holds the time.
Ṛ. The r that is a vowel, alongside the dot underneath that curls the tongue back for ṭ, ḍ, ṇ and ṣ.
Your line: let your tongue curl back for it. Today, when you meet a dot under a letter, let your tongue curl back for it once, even silently. Day one thousand forty-three.
